title: Croissant Pudding
subtitle: Leftover croissants in a rich custard, baked until puffed and golden
excerpt: Day-old croissants split, spread with raspberry jam, and baked in a cream and egg custard until puffed, deep gold, and set. The layered pastry crisps at the edges while the custard fills the interior.
sourceNotes: A modern variation on bread and butter pudding using croissants, popularised by British chefs in the 1990s and now a standard use for day-old croissants. The higher butter content in croissant pastry means the dish needs no buttering of the bread, the croissants bring their own richness.

content.text: Croissant pudding is bread and butter pudding made with croissants, richer and flakier, with layers of pastry that crisp at the exposed edges while the custard sets inside. A thin spread of jam between the cut halves gives a faint sweet-sharp seam through each serving. Day-old croissants work far better than fresh: fresh ones go entirely soft, while day-old hold their shape and absorb the custard more evenly. Bake at 170°C fan for 30 to 35 minutes until puffed and deep gold.

Preheat the oven to 170°C fan. Butter a 1.2-litre baking dish lightly. Spread the jam on the cut face of the bottom half of each croissant, then replace the top halves. Arrange the filled croissants cut-side up in the baking dish, pressing them in gently so they are snug but not crushed.

Whisk together the cream, milk, whole eggs, extra yolk, sugar, and vanilla in a large jug until smooth. Pour slowly over the croissants, letting the custard flow around and between them. Press the croissants down gently, the tops should remain exposed above the custard line to crisp during baking. Leave to soak for 15 minutes.

Bake at 170°C fan for 30 to 35 minutes until the croissants are puffed and deep gold and the custard is set with a very slight wobble in the very centre. The exposed pastry layers will have separated and crisped. Serve immediately from the dish, with cold cream poured alongside.

items.symptom: The croissants have gone completely soggy with no crust
items.cause: Fresh croissants were used instead of day-old, or the soak time was too long.
items.fix: Use croissants that are at least a day old and slightly dry to the touch. Keep the soak to 15 minutes, no longer.

items.symptom: The custard is still liquid after 35 minutes
items.cause: The oven temperature is running low.
items.fix: Return to the oven for a further 5 to 10 minutes. The custard should tremble rather than slosh when you nudge the dish.

items.symptom: The tops are over-browning before the custard sets
items.cause: The croissants were already very dark, or the oven runs hot at the top.
items.fix: Tent with foil for the last 10 minutes of baking.

content.text: Best eaten immediately, straight from the oven. The pudding softens and loses its crisp edges within an hour. Leftover portions can be eaten cold from the fridge within 1 day, they become more custardy as they cool and are pleasant cold, though nothing like the freshly baked version.
